21.0.s.en: 1. David compels Joab to number the people

21.0.0.en: 1 And Satan stood up against Israel, and provoked David to number Israel. 2 And David said to Joab and to the rulers of the people, “Go, number Israel from Beersheba even to Dan; and bring the number of them to me, that I may know it.” 3 And Joab answered, “The LORD make his people an hundred times so many more as they be: but, my lord the king, are they not all my lord’s servants? why then doth my lord require this thing? why will he be a cause of trespass to Israel?” 4 Nevertheless the king’s word prevailed against Joab. Wherefore Joab departed, and went throughout all Israel, and came to Jerusalem. 5 And Joab gave the sum of the number of the people unto David. And all they of Israel were a thousand thousand and an hundred thousand men that drew sword: and Judah was four hundred threescore and ten thousand men that drew sword. 6 But Levi and Benjamin counted he not among them: for the king’s word was abominable to Joab.

21.0.1.en: And Satan stood up against Israel, and provoked David to number Israel. [1]

21.0.2.en: Who was behind this sin? It is written in (2 Sam 24:1): “the anger of the LORD was kindled against Israel, and he moved David against them to say, Go, number Israel and Judah.” It is as though the Lord urged David to do it, because His anger had come upon the people. In the Book of Chronicles it is said that Satan was behind this act. Both are true, for God permitted Satan to tempt David. God is not the source of evil, but He permits it to accomplish His purposes. Satan offers the temptation, but he does not compel man to accept it.

21.0.3.en: It is evident here that Satan does not stand idly by before God’s plan and His continual works for accomplishing salvation. He tempted David’s heart in order to scatter God’s plans for His people. Satan tempted him as the serpent tempted Eve and Adam, and he also tried to tempt Job in order to destroy him (Job 1-2), and Zechariah the prophet saw him in one of the visions he beheld (Zech 3:1).

21.0.4.en: Numbering the people is not evil in itself, since it is fitting for a shepherd to know his flock. But it is clear that David sinned in this act and was the cause of God’s anger, because he did this out of pride of heart and lack of trust in God, relying on numbers. David carried out this census in order to boast of the strength of his army, to rely on his military capabilities rather than on God. The motive for his act was sin, namely vanity. Often sin lies not in our outward actions, but in our hidden motives.

21.0.5.en: We are certain that God does not cause sin, for “neither tempteth he any man.” Therefore, when it is said that He moved David to do it, it must be made clear that for a wise and holy purpose God permitted Satan to do it, and here we trace this erroneous course to its source and foundation. It is not strange that Satan, who is the enemy of God and of everything good, should stand against the people; for his aim is to destroy David and the people. Here we notice the following: 1. It is astonishing that Satan influences David to do something wrong, he who was a man whose heart was like God’s heart, for it would be supposed that he was among those whom the wicked one does not touch. God permitted this so that we may know that the holiest of the saints must not think that they are beyond the reach of Satan’s temptations. This reminds us of St. Macarius the Great, to whom Satan said, “You have arrived, O Macarius,” and he kept answering him, “I have not arrived,” until he gave up his spirit into the hand of his Creator, and then he said, “Now I have arrived.” Now when Satan intended to bring harm upon Israel, what way did he take? He did not [stir up God against them to swallow them up] (Job 2:3), but he stirred up David, their dearest friend, to number them, and thereby to anger God and provoke Him against them. 2. When Satan tempts us to sin against God, he harms us more than by his complaint against us before God. He destroys people by their own selves and their own hands. 3. The greatest harm Satan can do to the Church of God is to tempt its leaders with pride, because no one can see this sin in everyone, and especially in those who are foremost in the Church: “But ye shall not be so: but he that is greatest among you, let him be as the younger; and he that is chief, as he that doth serve” (Lk 22:26).

21.0.6.en: v David believed in You, and You took him from behind the sheep, and made him king, and he triumphed over Goliath and subdued all his persecutors.

21.0.7.en: The devil stirred up his forces against him from every side, but because Your right hand held his hand, he persevered and received courage.

21.0.8.en: The wicked one put it into his heart to number the nation, so the Lord disciplined him with mercy and received him with love (2 Sam 24).

21.0.9.en: He made him king, and filled him with the spirit of prophecy, and the wealth of his words overflowed and filled all creation.

21.1.0.en: He became a fountain, from which the words of the Holy Spirit burst forth, and the peoples and the worlds drank from it, and they are still thirsty for them [2].

21.2.0.en: And David said to Joab and to the rulers of the people,

21.2.1.en: “Go, number Israel from Beersheba even to Dan; and bring the number of them to me, that I may know it.” [2]

21.3.0.en: And Joab answered, “The LORD make his people an hundred times so many more as they be:

21.3.1.en: but, my lord the king, are they not all my lord’s servants?

21.3.2.en: why then doth my lord require this thing?

21.3.3.en: why will he be a cause of trespass to Israel?” [3]

21.3.4.en: This story highlights David’s fall into a weakness that no one expected, which led Joab to rebuke David for it. David sinned because he relied on the arm of his people, contrary to his custom, and sought the glory of himself.

21.3.5.en: The Lord Himself had warned him when He said to him by the mouth of Nathan the prophet: [I was with thee whithersoever thou hast walked, and have cut off all thine enemies from before thee, and have made thee a name like the name of the great men that are in the earth] (1 Chr 17:8).

21.3.6.en: David did not consult God before carrying out the census, nor did he heed Joab’s advice. For Joab was against the idea of taking a census, and did not take the order David issued in this matter seriously.

21.3.7.en: Joab, whom David used, was a man of standing in public affairs, but he was compelled to this task, and did it with the utmost reluctance imaginable. He lodged a protest against this work before he began it, for there was no man more advanced than he in anything that tended to the glory of the king and the good of the kingdom, but in this matter he wished gladly to be excused, for two reasons: 1. He saw that there was no need for it and no occasion for it, for God had promised to multiply His people, and Joab had no question about the fulfillment of this promise; all the people were the king’s servants and he had no doubt of their loyalty and love for him. 2. This matter was dangerous, and carrying it out might cause a trespass for Israel and perhaps stir up God’s anger against them. Joab understood this, but David did not understand it, so consultation in a spirit of humility was necessary.

21.4.0.en: Nevertheless the king’s word prevailed against Joab.

21.4.1.en: Wherefore Joab departed, and went throughout all Israel, and came to Jerusalem. [4]

21.4.2.en: He was troubled by this matter before he undertook it: “for the king’s word was abominable to Joab.” Everything King David had done before this was good in the eyes of all the people (2 Sam 3:36), but now there was a general aversion to these orders, which confirmed Joab’s hatred of them.

21.5.0.en: And Joab gave the sum of the number of the people unto David. And all they of Israel were a thousand thousand (a million) and an hundred thousand men that drew sword: and Judah was four hundred threescore and ten thousand men that drew sword. [5]

21.5.1.en: Although the result of this review was very great, Joab had no heart to complete it, and he left two important tribes without being numbered, namely the tribes of Levi and Benjamin [5-6]. Perhaps he was not careful in numbering the other tribes, because he did the work grudgingly, which explains the difference between the figures of the census and what is recorded in (2 Sam 24:9).

21.5.2.en: The difference in the figures of the census here and in (2 Sam 24) is due to the fact that 2 Samuel does not count the standing army mentioned in (1 Chr 28), which also adds the captains of hundreds and the captains of thousands. For David did not want to know the number of the regular army, since he knew it well in general terms, but he wanted to know the extent to which the strength of Israel could reach, so that he might use it on any possible occasion.

21.6.0.en: But Levi and Benjamin counted he not among them: for the king’s word was abominable to Joab. [6]

21.6.1.en: The tribe of Levi was not numbered because they are not subject to compulsory conscription, and because the tribe was scattered among the rest of the tribes, and it was difficult to gather the number of the Levites. Benjamin was not numbered, because the census was disrupted before reaching Benjamin (1 Chr 27:24), on account of the spread of the plague.

21.6.2.en: There is a great contrast between this incident and what happened to David the young shepherd when he came to the field of battle and saw Goliath the giant strutting about arrogantly and taunting Israel. That little shepherd did not wish to take a census and did not number the army, but it is written in his psalms: “It is better to trust in the LORD than to put confidence in man. It is better to trust in the LORD than to put confidence in princes” (Ps 118:8-9). He said, [Let me face him](*). Why did he have the courage to do so? Because he trusted in the Lord. And he learned the lesson from the incident of the census.

21.6.3.en: v Great is the power of hope in the Lord: an unconquerable fortress, a protecting wall that cannot be attacked, a military reinforcement that is not defeated, a quiet harbor, a strong tower, an irresistible weapon, an unconquerable strength able to find a refuge in a place no one expects. By this power the unarmed become armed, the condition of women becomes better than that of men, and children prove that they easily become stronger than those who practice the arts of war. What wonder is it if they overcome enemies, when in reality they overcome the world itself?... Hope in the Lord changes everything! [3]

21.6.4.en: v He did not say, “I shall not suffer,” but “I will not fear what man shall do unto me,” meaning that although I suffer, I do not fear, as Paul also said: “If God be for us, who can be against us?” (Rom 8:31). In reality there were countless things against him, but he did not use them wrongly... He was higher and loftier above all fears...

21.6.5.en: God loves you, my dear ones, and therefore He draws you away from everything... and pulls you to Himself [4].

21.6.6.en: St. John Chrysostom v They say: Why does (divine providence) not support you when you are persecuted?... What evil can befall us as long as we look to death as a departure, by which we go to the Lord, as though it were a change of life, we pass from one life to another life?!...

21.6.7.en: Each of us says with confidence: [The LORD is on my side; I will not fear: what can man do unto me?] (Ps 118:6). [But the souls of the righteous are in the hand of God, and there shall no torment touch them] (Wis 3:1)... They persecute us not because we are evildoers, but they think that we Christians sin against life, and that we act against ourselves [5].

21.6.8.en: St. Clement of Alexandria v Before the war begins, seek an ally; before falling ill, let you have your physician; before sorrowful things come upon you, pray, for in the time of your sorrows you will find Him, and He will hear you [6].

21.6.9.en: Mar Isaac the Syrian And we must ask ourselves this important question: Do we always believe and trust in the Lord? “But without faith it is impossible to please him...” (Heb 11:6). And the Lord Jesus, glory be to Him, said: [When the Holy Spirit is come, he will reprove the world of sin]. What sin...? “Because they believe not on me” (Jn 16:8-9), and St. Paul the Apostle said: “For whatsoever is not of faith is sin” (Rom 14:23). This was David’s sin in that incident, and he soon realized the extent of the error into which he had fallen in this matter.

21.7.s.en: 2. David’s repentance for what he had done

21.7.0.en: 7 And God was displeased with this thing; therefore he smote Israel. 8 And David said unto God, “I have sinned greatly, because I have done this thing: but now, I beseech thee, do away the iniquity of thy servant; for I have done very foolishly.”

21.7.1.en: And God was displeased with this thing; therefore he smote Israel. [7]

21.7.2.en: In the census the ransom commanded in (Ex 30:12) was not collected. And David’s pride and disobedience brought grave consequences.

21.7.3.en: v The conduct of rulers is often tied to the characteristics of those subject to them, so that even those who are truly good shepherds sin as a result of the evil of their flock. For David the prophet, who was praised by the testimony of God Himself, and who was qualified to know heavenly mysteries, was puffed up with sudden pride, and sinned by numbering the people. And although it was he who sinned, the people fell under the punishment. Why? Because in truth the hearts of rulers are affected by the deserts of their peoples.

21.7.4.en: The godly judge (David) was rebuked for the sinner’s error by having a punishment imposed on the very persons on whose account he himself had sinned...

21.7.5.en: Since he fell into pride with full freedom of his will, he fell under punishment for his sin. For this severe wrath that struck the people in their bodies wore down the ruler of the people with pain in the depths of his heart. Surely the deserts of rulers and people are shared and interlinked, since the conduct of the people often becomes evil because of the error of their shepherds, and the conduct of the shepherds changes according to the deserts of their people [7].

21.8.0.en: And David said unto God, “I have sinned greatly, because I have done this thing.

21.8.1.en: but now, I beseech thee, do away the iniquity of thy servant; for I have done very foolishly.” [8]

21.8.2.en: When David realized his sin and its gravity, he took responsibility, and was quickly broken, confessing his error before the Lord and asking Him to forgive him.

21.8.3.en: He confessed his sin sincerely and prayed for its forgiveness [8]. He confessed that he had sinned greatly, and that he had done this thing very foolishly, and he besought that the iniquity be removed.

21.8.4.en: v When David ordered the numbering of the people, he was greatly smitten in his heart, and said: [I have sinned greatly, because I have done this thing: but now, I beseech thee, O LORD, do away the iniquity of thy servant; for I have done very foolishly] (see 1 Chr 21:8). And Nathan the prophet was sent (to him) again to choose (one of the chastisements)... David said that these three (chastisements) are great calamities for me, but I fall into the hand of the Lord, for His mercies are very great, and I do not fall into the hands of men.

21.8.5.en: David’s error was that he desired to know the numbers of all the people who were with him; this knowledge should have been left to God alone.

21.8.6.en: It is said that when the plague came upon the people on the first day at supper time, David, seeing the angel smiting the people, said: [I the shepherd have sinned, and have done evil, but these sheep, what have they done? Let thine hand be on me, and on my father’s house]. Then the Lord repented, and commanded the angel to spare the people, and that David should offer a sacrifice, since sacrifices at that time were offered for sin, but now they are sacrifices of repentance. Thus by his humility he became more acceptable to God. For it is not strange that men should err, but they deserve rebuke if they do not know that they have sinned and so do not humble themselves before God [8].

21.9.0.en: 9 And the LORD spake unto Gad, David’s seer, saying, 10 “Go and tell David, saying, Thus saith the LORD, I offer thee three things: choose thee one of them, that I may do it unto thee.” 11 So Gad came to David, and said unto him, “Thus saith the LORD, Choose thee 12 Either three years’ famine; or three months to be destroyed before thy foes, while that the sword of thine enemies overtaketh thee; or else three days the sword of the LORD, even the pestilence, in the land, and the angel of the LORD destroying throughout all the coasts of Israel. Now therefore advise thyself what word I shall bring again to him that sent me.” 13 And David said unto Gad, “I am in a great strait: let me fall now into the hand of the LORD; for very great are his mercies: but let me not fall into the hand of man.”

21.9.1.en: And the LORD spake unto Gad, David’s seer: [9]

21.10.0.en: “Go and tell David, saying, Thus saith the LORD,

21.10.1.en: I offer thee three things: choose thee one of them, that I may do it unto thee.” [10]

21.11.0.en: So Gad came to David, and said unto him,

21.12.0.en: Either three years’ famine; or three months to be destroyed before thy foes, while that the sword of thine enemies overtaketh thee; or else three days the sword of the LORD, even the pestilence, in the land, and the angel of the LORD destroying throughout all the coasts of Israel.

21.12.1.en: Now therefore advise thyself what word I shall bring again to him that sent me.” [12]

21.12.2.en: David fell under the rod of chastisement because of the numbering of the people. This rod of chastisement drives foolishness out of the heart, the foolishness of pride and of relying on numbers instead of trusting in God, and let us consider the following: 1. David realized that this thing was evil in the eyes of God [9-11], and this is no light matter for a good man like David. The Lord looks and takes no pleasure in the sin of His people, and there is no sin more displeasing to God than pride of heart and lack of trust in God; likewise nothing is more grievous and deadly to a sensitive soul than to be an object of God’s displeasure.

21.12.3.en: It is profitable for us to notice how God focuses on certain things in David’s life, for many here consider that some attitudes are sin and other attitudes are not sin or are less wrong, but when we stand in God’s presence we shall discover that our view was mistaken in this respect, and we shall know the meaning of sin. We must know that sin is not only in deeds, that is, the things we do or do not do, but also in thoughts and intentions, and by studying the word of God we know His view of sin. 2. David was given the choice of one punishment out of three: war, famine, or pestilence, and thereby God permits him to be humbled for the sake of his repentance and the salvation of his soul all the more; he was placed in a very difficult position before the dread of three punishments, without doubt amid his great bewilderment when he considered which of the three to choose.

21.13.0.en: And David said unto Gad, “I am in a great strait:

21.13.1.en: let me fall now into the hand of the LORD; for very great are his mercies: but let me not fall into the hand of man.” [13]

21.13.2.en: When the opportunity to choose the chastisement was offered to him, he preferred falling into the hand of the Lord to falling into the hand of man, because he knew that He is merciful.

21.14.s.en: 4. The pestilence and the deliverance of Jerusalem from it

21.14.0.en: 14 So the LORD sent pestilence upon Israel: and there fell of Israel seventy thousand men. 15 And God sent an angel unto Jerusalem to destroy it: and as he was destroying, the LORD beheld, and he repented him of the evil, and said to the angel that destroyed, “It is enough, stay now thine hand.” And the angel of the LORD stood by the threshingfloor of Ornan the Jebusite. 16 And David lifted up his eyes, and saw the angel of the LORD stand between the earth and the heaven, having a drawn sword in his hand stretched out over Jerusalem. Then David and the elders of Israel, who were clothed in sackcloth, fell upon their faces. 17 And David said unto God, “Is it not I that commanded the people to be numbered? even I it is that have sinned and done evil indeed; but as for these sheep, what have they done? let thine hand, I pray thee, O LORD my God, be on me, and on my father’s house; but not on thy people, that they should be plagued.”

21.14.1.en: So the LORD sent pestilence upon Israel: and there fell of Israel seventy thousand men. [14]

21.14.2.en: Sin has a chain effect, for it drags behind it a series of consequences. When we remember the consequences that will come upon us, sin becomes bitter in our mouth and we reject it.

21.14.3.en: Within a few hours David heard of the fall of seventy thousand of his subjects, who died by the pestilence. He had been proud of the abundance of his people, but the divine chastisement took its course to make them fewer in number; for justly that in which we boast is taken from us, so that we fall into weakness and feel its bitter taste. David had insisted on numbering his people and said: “Go, number Israel... and bring the number of them to me, that I may know it” [2], but now God numbers them in another way: “Therefore will I number you to the sword...” (Isa 65:12), and they brought David another number, which was to his confusion and not to his delight, for he counted those who perished by the sword of the angel, the black document of death, which was a blow to the register of David’s soldiers.

21.14.4.en: The commission of sin drags behind it a series of grave consequences; 70,000 people were killed before the plague ceased.

21.14.5.en: Often the community suffers because of the leader’s error, but on the Day of the Lord every person will be judged for his own personal error.

21.14.6.en: Perhaps someone may ask why God permitted the death of seventy thousand of the people because of David’s sin?

21.14.7.en: St. Jerome says that a person often wonders why God permitted the destruction of seventy thousand men because of the error of one man, David? And why did He permit the destruction of many because of the error of Achan the son of Carmi (Josh 7)? And why did the Lord Christ delay His coming for the salvation of the world? And so on. He answers that we try to defend God and justify His actions, but who is man that he should comprehend the wisdom of God and His plan: [Leave to God’s authority the sovereignty over your own authority, for He has no need of you to justify His actions [9].]

21.14.8.en: St. Ambrose presents us with many questions concerning the judgments of God. It is hard for man to comprehend God’s plan, because His judgments are loftier than ours. He says: [Will you too condescend...? Let God have His authority over what is His. He has no need of you to justify His works [10].]

21.14.9.en: v In truth I have already said that the crime of one person was the cause of the destruction of many of God’s people, just as the people were shattered because of the theft of Achan (Josh 7), and the plague that came because of the envy of King Saul(**), as death came because of the numbering of the people by the saint David (1 Sam 14; 1 Chr 21).

21.14.10.en: The Church of God is like the eye, and just as a speck of dirt, however small, when it falls on the eye may harm the sight, so in the same way, if some commit unclean deeds, however few they may be in the body of the Church, they hinder the radiant light of the Church [11].

21.15.0.en: And God sent an angel unto Jerusalem to destroy it: and as he was destroying, the LORD beheld, and he repented him of the evil, and said to the angel that destroyed, “It is enough, stay now thine hand.”

21.15.1.en: And the angel of the LORD stood by the threshingfloor of Ornan the Jebusite. [15]

21.15.2.en: Here we see the end of the matter, for as soon as David repented, his peace with God returned to him: [O LORD, I will praise thee: though thou wast angry with me, thine anger is turned away] (Isa 12:1). The Lord set a limit to the advance of destruction [15], and when David repented of this sin, the Lord repented of the evil sentence and commanded the destroying angel to stay his hand and return his sword to its sheath [27]. The sword of judgment was returned to its sheath, but at Calvary the sword pierced the side of our Lord Jesus Christ, and as one student said: “I entered into the heart of God through the wound of a spear.”

21.16.0.en: And David lifted up his eyes, and saw the angel of the LORD stand between the earth and the heaven, having a drawn sword in his hand stretched out over Jerusalem.

21.16.1.en: Then David and the elders of Israel, who were clothed in sackcloth, fell upon their faces. [16]

21.16.2.en: David saw the destroying angel with his sword stretched out over Jerusalem [16], and this caused him great terror, because it was a sign of the wrath of heaven and a threat of destroying that beloved city. If the sight of an angel coming on a peaceful mission has made the greatest of men tremble, how much more the sight of an angel with a drawn sword in his hand, a fiery sword like that of the cherubim which turned every way to keep the way of the tree of life. When we are under God’s wrath, the pure angels who rejoice over a repentant sinner are against us, but we do not see them as David saw.

21.17.0.en: And David said unto God, “Is it not I that commanded the people to be numbered?

21.17.1.en: even I it is that have sinned and done evil indeed;

21.17.2.en: but as for these sheep, what have they done?

21.17.3.en: let thine hand, I pray thee, O LORD my God, be on me, and on my father’s house; but not on thy people, that they should be plagued.” [17]

21.17.4.en: By David’s saying this to God, he presents a practical example of love with humility. In his discourse on release from death, St. Ambrose presented to us the petition of David the prophet to God that His hand be on him and on his father’s house, and not on the people, as a practical example of accepting death as a chastisement for the release of the soul from sin.

21.17.5.en: v Since the Apostle teaches us that the person who departs from his body is with Christ, provided he is worthy of this, let us contemplate the nature of life and death. We know from the teaching of Holy Scripture that death is the release of the soul from the body, a kind of separation in man. For we are freed from this bond between soul and body when we depart...

21.17.6.en: He (David) offered himself to death to atone for his disobedience to the Lord, and offered himself ready to bear the vengeance of God for the sake of the rest of his suffering people.

21.17.7.en: He knew that he would be more glorious when he died for the sake of Christ than when he reigned in this world (as a king), for what is greater than that a man should become an offering for the sake of Christ? [13]

21.17.8.en: St. Ambrose wrote St. Ambrose in his letter to the Emperor Theodosius, encouraging him to repent of what he had committed in the massacre of Thessalonica about the year 390 A.D., and asks him to imitate King David, who sinned, but offered repentance for what he had done.

21.17.9.en: David accepted the punishment for his iniquity: “let thine hand be on me, and on my father’s house” [17] [I place myself under the rod of chastisement, so let me suffer alone, for I am the one who sinned and did evil, and I am the guilty head against which the sword must be drawn].

21.17.10.en: He cast himself on God’s mercy, although he knew that God was angry with him, and no evil thought against God came to his mind, for whatever happens, “let me fall now into the hand of the LORD; for very great are his mercies” [13]. For the good man thinks well of God even if the world frowns in his face: [Though He lead me to the slaughter, I trust in Him].

21.17.11.en: He showed tender feeling and concern for his people, and his heart was pricked when he saw them smitten because of his transgression: “but as for these sheep, what have they done?” [17].

21.17.12.en: It was not easy for David to see the angel of the Lord drawing his sword against his people who were beloved to him, and against the city of Jerusalem, which had its special place in his heart.

21.17.14.en: a. He confessed his sin and asked the Lord with all his heart for pardon [8]. He confessed that he had acted foolishly and had made himself a fool.

21.17.15.en: b. He accepted chastisement from God’s hand for his sin [17], with all submission.

21.17.16.en: c. He cast himself on God’s mercy although he knew that God was angry with him [13].

21.17.17.en: d. He showed tenderness toward his people, and suffered exceedingly when he realized that what had befallen his people was because of his sin.

21.17.18.en: We are not surprised if God permits the chastisement of many because of a sin committed by a very few, perhaps by one person. For God wants His Church to be holy and without blemish. He permits temporary collective chastisement, because on the great Day of the Lord, each one will give an account of his own personal work. But here the general chastisement is permitted by the Lord as a practical sermon to all.

21.17.19.en: Pope Gregory (the Great) [14] sees that the characters of leaders are tied to the condition of those subject to them. They are often good people, but unfortunately they change because of the authority given to them. As Samuel the prophet said to King Saul that the Lord says to him: “When thou wast little in thine own sight, wast thou not made the head of the tribes of Israel, and the LORD anointed thee king over Israel?” (1 Sam 15:17).

21.17.20.en: v David tended his father’s flock, and was taken from the flock to shepherd his people. “So he fed them according to the integrity of his heart; and guided them by the skilfulness of his hands” (Ps 78:72). And when David numbered his flock, wrath came upon them, and they began to perish. Then David surrendered himself to be accountable for his flock when he prayed, saying: [Lo, I have sinned, and I have done wickedly: but these sheep, what have they done? let thine hand, I pray thee, be against me, and against my father’s house] (2 Sam 24:17).

21.17.21.en: So also all watchful shepherds are accustomed to give themselves up on behalf of their flock [15].

21.17.22.en: St. Aphrahat v Good is humility. It saves those in danger and raises up the fallen. Humility was known from the one who said: “Lo, I have sinned, and I have done wickedly: but these sheep, what have they done? let thine hand, I pray thee, be against me, and against my father’s house” (see 2 Sam 24:17; 1 Chr 21:17). Well does David say this, he who made his kingdom subject to God, and offered repentance, and confessed his sin, and asked for pardon. He obtained salvation by humility!

21.17.23.en: Christ Himself was humble, and whoever follows the humility of Christ finds rest in Christ [16].

21.17.24.en: v So by his humility (David) became more acceptable to God, for it is not strange that the people should err, but they are blamed if they do not realize that they have sinned and so do not humble themselves before God [17].

21.17.25.en: St. Ambrose v What do you say of David, who received a great testimony from God, for He said of him: [I have found a man after mine own heart, David the son of Jesse; with my holy oil have I anointed him] (Ps 89:21).

21.17.26.en: This very man says to God: [Have mercy upon me, O God, according to thy lovingkindness: according unto the multitude of thy tender mercies blot out my transgressions] (Ps 51:1-17).

21.17.27.en: Wash me thoroughly from mine iniquity, and cleanse me from my sin. For I acknowledge my transgressions: and my sin is ever before me.

21.17.28.en: Against thee, thee only, have I sinned, and done this evil in thy sight: that thou mightest be justified when thou speakest, and be clear when thou judgest.

21.17.29.en: Behold, I was shapen in iniquity; and in sin did my mother conceive me.

21.17.30.en: Behold, thou desirest truth in the inward parts: and in the hidden part thou shalt make me to know wisdom.

21.17.31.en: Purge me with hyssop, and I shall be clean: wash me, and I shall be whiter than snow.

21.17.32.en: Make me to hear joy and gladness; that the bones which thou hast broken may rejoice.

21.17.33.en: Hide thy face from my sins, and blot out all mine iniquities.

21.17.34.en: Create in me a clean heart, O God; and renew a right spirit within me.

21.17.35.en: Cast me not away from thy presence; and take not thy holy spirit from me.

21.17.36.en: Restore unto me the joy of thy salvation; and uphold me with thy free (leading) spirit.

21.17.37.en: Then will I teach transgressors thy ways; and sinners shall be converted unto thee. Deliver me from bloodguiltiness, O God, thou God of my salvation: and my tongue shall sing aloud of thy righteousness.

21.17.38.en: O Lord, open thou my lips; and my mouth shall shew forth thy praise.

21.17.39.en: For thou desirest not sacrifice; else would I give it: thou delightest not in burnt offering.

21.18.0.en: The sacrifices of God are a broken spirit: a broken and a contrite heart, O God, thou wilt not despise [18].

21.19.s.en: 5. The building of an altar at the threshingfloor of Ornan

21.19.0.en: 18 Then the angel of the LORD commanded Gad to say to David, that David should go up, and set up an altar unto the LORD in the threshingfloor of Ornan the Jebusite. 19 And David went up at the saying of Gad, which he spake in the name of the LORD. 20 And Ornan turned back, and saw the angel; and his four sons with him hid themselves. Now Ornan was threshing wheat. 21 And as David came to Ornan, Ornan looked and saw David, and went out of the threshingfloor, and bowed himself to David with his face to the ground. 22 Then David said to Ornan, “Grant me the place of this threshingfloor, that I may build an altar therein unto the LORD: thou shalt grant it me for the full price: that the plague may be stayed from the people.” 23 And Ornan said unto David, “Take it to thee, and let my lord the king do that which is good in his eyes: lo, I give thee the oxen also for burnt offerings, and the threshing instruments for wood, and the wheat for the meat offering; I give it all.” 24 And king David said to Ornan, “Nay; but I will verily buy it for the full price: for I will not take that which is thine for the LORD, nor offer burnt offerings without cost.” 25 So David gave to Ornan for the place six hundred shekels of gold by weight. 26 And David built there an altar unto the LORD, and offered burnt offerings and peace offerings, and called upon the LORD; and he answered him from heaven by fire upon the altar of burnt offering. 27 And the LORD commanded the angel; and he put up his sword again into the sheath thereof. 28 At that time when David saw that the LORD had answered him in the threshingfloor of Ornan the Jebusite, then he sacrificed there. 29 For the tabernacle of the LORD, which Moses made in the wilderness, and the altar of the burnt offering, were at that season in the high place at Gibeon. 30 But David could not go before it to enquire of God: for he was afraid because of the sword of the angel of the LORD.

21.19.1.en: Then the angel of the LORD commanded Gad to say to David, that David should go up, and set up an altar unto the LORD in the threshingfloor of Ornan the Jebusite. [18]

21.19.2.en: Instructions were given to David to build an altar to the Lord at the threshingfloor of Ornan [18], and the angel commanded Gad the prophet to bring these instructions to David. The very angel who carried out the war in the name of the Lord here brings the step leading to peace. For the angels do not want us to grieve.

21.19.3.en: The angel could have brought these instructions to David directly, but he brought them through the seer, in order to show the honor of the prophets.

21.19.4.en: Likewise the Revelation of Jesus Christ, which God gave to John the Apostle by the hand of an angel, and from him to the churches.

21.19.5.en: The instructions to David to set up the altar were a blessed symbol of reconciliation, for if God had been pleased with his death, He would not have accepted the sacrifice from his hands.

21.19.6.en: On the mount of the mirrors, grace met righteousness.

21.20.0.en: v Observe, brethren, that there is no place in the land of the Jews worthy for the temple of the Lord to be built in it, but in the land of the Gentiles there is a chosen place; where the angel was seen, the altar was built, and by this the wrath of the Lord was appeased. This signifies that the hearts of the Jews were not found qualified for sacrifices to be offered in them, but the land of the Gentiles, that is, the conscience of Christians, is chosen as the place for the temple of the Lord. This is what the Apostle clearly indicates when he rebuked the Jews, saying: “It was necessary that the word of God should first have been spoken to you: but seeing ye put it from you, and judge yourselves unworthy of everlasting life, lo, we turn to the Gentiles” (Acts 13:46)... This is the reason the angel of the Lord stood at the threshingfloor of the Gentile king, for the true Angel, Christ, visited the Gentile peoples [19].

21.21.0.en: Father Caesarius, Bishop of Arles v Here too the angel held his sword, and while he was destroying the whole city of the wicked, he pointed to the temple of the Lord at the threshingfloor of Ornan, king of the Jebusites. Thus he showed beforehand that the Church of Christ grows not in Israel, but among the Gentiles [20].

21.22.0.en: And David went up at the saying of Gad, which he spake in the name of the LORD. [19]

21.23.0.en: And Ornan turned back, and saw the angel;

21.23.1.en: and his four sons with him hid themselves. Now Ornan was threshing wheat. [20]

21.23.2.en: David hastened to make an agreement with Ornan for the threshingfloor because he does not serve God at the expense of others, although Ornan offered it to him freely, not only out of kindness toward the king, but because he saw the angel [20], which aroused terror in him and his four sons, and they all hid themselves. For they could not bear the splendor of his glory, and they feared his drawn sword. His fear of the evil to come made him ready to do anything for the sake of atonement, for all who have a keen sense of the fear of God promote repentance, and encourage every way of reconciliation for the turning back of God’s wrath.

21.24.0.en: And as David came to Ornan,

21.24.1.en: Ornan looked and saw David, and went out of the threshingfloor, and bowed himself to David with his face to the ground. [21]

21.25.0.en: Then David said to Ornan, “Grant me the place of this threshingfloor, that I may build an altar therein unto the LORD:

21.25.1.en: thou shalt grant it me for the full price: that the plague may be stayed from the people.” [22]

21.26.0.en: And Ornan said unto David, “Take it to thee, and let my lord the king do that which is good in his eyes:

21.26.1.en: lo, I give thee the oxen also for burnt offerings, and the threshing instruments for wood, and the wheat for the meat offering;

21.27.0.en: And king David said to Ornan, “Nay; but I will verily buy it for the full price: for I will not take that which is thine for the LORD, nor offer burnt offerings without cost.” [24]

21.27.1.en: The burnt offering here means offering the whole heart to God, and also offering time or money or what we possess. Therefore David wanted to offer everything from his own money, and not from the money of others.

21.27.2.en: v Araunah offered to the blessed David the threshingfloor and the ox as a burnt sacrifice, but King David refused to accept them unless he first paid the price. This too was fulfilled at the coming of our Lord and Savior, for He refused to take the hearts of the Gentiles for Himself unless He paid His precious blood for them [21], Father Caesarius, Bishop of Arles

21.28.0.en: So David gave to Ornan for the place six hundred shekels of gold by weight. [25]

21.28.1.en: The Book of Samuel mentions that the price of the oxen and the threshingfloor was very small, so David paid 50 shekels of silver (2 Sam 24:24), but the Book of Chronicles here makes clear that David bought the whole place (Hebrew hammaqom), which includes the entire area of Mount Moriah, so he paid 600 shekels of gold.

21.28.2.en: The purchase of this large area may have come at a later stage, after the purchase of the threshingfloor of wheat and the oxen that David used in the first sacrifice.

21.28.3.en: Perhaps the difference between the first and second purchase explains to us why Araunah offered at the outset to give David the threshingfloor of wheat. For it is hard to suppose that he was in a position that allowed him to give the whole of Mount Moriah, but he gives the threshingfloor only.

21.29.0.en: And David built there an altar unto the LORD, and offered burnt offerings and peace offerings, and called upon the LORD; and he answered him from heaven by fire upon the altar of burnt offering. [26]

21.29.1.en: King David refused to take the threshingfloor of Ornan the Jebusite to set up an altar on it freely, for he does not offer to the Lord what belongs to the money of others.

21.29.2.en: God showed His acceptance of David’s offerings on this altar, “and he answered him from heaven by fire” [26]. The proof that God’s wrath had been lifted from him is that instead of the fire justly settling on the sinner, it settled on the sacrifice and consumed it, and this was followed by the returning of the destroying sword to its sheath. Likewise Christ was made sin and a curse for us, for it pleased the Lord to bruise Him, so that God might be to us through Him not a consuming fire but a reconciled Father.

21.30.0.en: And the LORD commanded the angel; and he put up his sword again into the sheath thereof. [27]

21.31.0.en: At that time when David saw that the LORD had answered him in the threshingfloor of Ornan the Jebusite, then he sacrificed there. [28]

21.32.0.en: David continued offering his sacrifices on this altar, for the bronze altar that Moses had made was at that time in the high place at Gibeon [29], and Israel’s sacrifices were offered there. But David was afraid because of seeing the sword of the angel, so that he could not go to Gibeon to enquire of God [30], for the matter called for haste when the pestilence began. Aaron had to hasten, indeed run, to make atonement (Num 16:46-47). And the situation here was no less urgent, for time did not allow David, lest the fatal blow come before his return. Therefore God commanded him, out of pity for him, to set up an altar in that place, and God granted him a dispensation from His own law concerning the one altar because of the present trial, and permitted sacrifices to be offered on this altar, which was not set up in opposition to the one at Gibeon but alongside it, for the emblems of unity were not barred any more than unity itself, and even after the present trial had passed (as is apparent) David continued to offer sacrifices here although the altar at Gibeon continued, because God approved the sacrifices offered on the altar at the threshingfloor of Ornan and confirmed His acceptance of them [28].

21.33.0.en: For the tabernacle of the LORD, which Moses made in the wilderness, and the altar of the burnt offering, were at that season in the high place at Gibeon. [29]

21.33.1.en: God chose the site of the threshingfloor of Ornan the Jebusite on Mount Moriah, the place where God commanded Abraham to offer his son as a sacrifice, looking forward to the time of the sacrifices of the temple, and finally the sacrifice of the Lamb of God who taketh away the sin of the world. So David built this altar where the temple would be built and sacrifice would be offered, and this is the place where God meets with His people, and it has now become the place of sacrifice.

21.33.2.en: David set up this altar, and offered a burnt sacrifice, which points to the person of Christ, and then offered a peace offering, and this also points to Christ our peace. For Christ made peace by the shedding of His blood on the Cross, and He is our peace, and it is He whose blood was sprinkled on the mercy seat for us. And He is our great High Priest, and He ascended into the heavens and is seated at the right hand of the Father, for there is no access to the Father except through our Lord Jesus Christ, the Mediator of the covenant. David realized this by the spirit of prophecies, and offered the burnt sacrifice and the peace offering to God.
